record.paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
record.original_question: Is the discrepancy between predicted and observed mass assembly of brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) a real failure of the models, or can it be explained by mismatched comparisons such as observational aperture magnitudes versus model total magnitudes and by the omission in many semi-analytic models of spatial light distributions and tidal stripping into intracluster light?

evidence.quote: For the mass assembly of the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs), the situation is worse: while observations seem consistent with no mass growth since z ∼ 1, models predict an increase in mass by a factor about 4 [23, 26].

One major caveat in this comparison is given by the fact that observational studies usually adopt fixed metric aperture magnitudes (which account for 25-50 per cent of the total light contained in the BCG and intra-cluster light), while models compute total magnitudes.
In addition, most of the available models do not take into account the stripping of stars from other cluster galaxies due to tidal and harassment effects [27, 28].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let a brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) be the most luminous galaxy at the centre of a galaxy cluster, and let intracluster light (ICL) denote the diffuse stellar component bound to the cluster potential rather than to any single galaxy. Observations of BCGs typically measure stellar masses inside a fixed metric aperture, which is known to capture only roughly 25–50% of the combined BCG+ICL light, whereas semi-analytic models of galaxy formation generally output total stellar masses for the BCG and often do not track tidal stripping of stars from satellite galaxies into the ICL.

Standard semi-analytic predictions are that the stellar mass of a BCG grows by approximately a factor of 4 between redshift z ≈ 1 and z = 0, while observations using fixed-aperture magnitudes are consistent with little or no mass growth over the same interval.

Determine whether this discrepancy reflects a genuine failure of the underlying galaxy-formation models, or whether it can be fully accounted for by:
(i) the systematic mismatch between fixed-aperture observational stellar masses and total model stellar masses, and
(ii) the omission, in most semi-analytic models, of an explicit treatment of the spatial light distribution of central galaxies and of the tidal/harassment-driven stripping of stars from cluster members into the ICL.

Specifically, formulate and justify a quantitative comparison procedure (matching apertures and including stripping into ICL) under which the predicted and observed BCG stellar-mass growth between z ≈ 1 and z = 0 either agree within observational uncertainties (resolving the discrepancy) or remain inconsistent (confirming a model failure).
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work suggests the discrepancy is largely, but not entirely, attributable to the comparison mismatch and omitted physics. Modern semi-analytic and hydrodynamical models that explicitly track tidal stripping into ICL and apply matched apertures bring predicted BCG stellar-mass growth much closer to observed values, with the BCG+ICL system continuing to grow strongly while the aperture-restricted BCG mass grows only modestly. However, a residual tension remains: some recent observations still find faster stellar-mass growth in the central regions than models predict, so a complete reconciliation has not been firmly established.

status_evidence.title: The Growth of Brightest Cluster Galaxies and Intracluster Light Over the Past Ten Billion Years
status_evidence.snippet: Semi-analytic models including ICL find that ICL growth is delayed relative to BCG growth, so BCG+ICL grows substantially since z=1; observations show less BCG mass evolution, partly due to aperture choices.
status_evidence.claim: Aperture choice and inclusion of ICL strongly affect the comparison and partially reconcile model predictions with observations.

status_evidence.title: The hierarchical growth of bright central galaxies and intracluster light as traced by the magnitude gap
status_evidence.snippet: Models that couple semi-analytic galaxy formation with N-body simulations and explicitly model BCG+ICL stellar distributions in different apertures study the reliability of growth predictions.
status_evidence.claim: Modern models incorporate spatial light distributions and stripping into ICL, addressing the original caveats.

status_evidence.title: Brightest cluster galaxies are statistically special from z = 0.3 to z = 1
status_evidence.snippet: Stellar mass within central 100 kpc increases by a factor of 3.8 from z=1.5 to z=0, more than twice the physical halo mass growth.
status_evidence.claim: Residual tension remains between observed central stellar-mass growth and model predictions even with aperture matching.
